vignette:
Amara

Amara was sixty-eight when the war came to her village in South Sudan. She had spent thirty years as a forester, walking the acacia groves and managing the timber cooperatives that sustained her community. She knew the land the way other people knew their own homes—every path, every seasonal shift in the light filtering through the canopy. Her husband, Daniel, had died five years before the conflict, and their two adult children had long since moved to Khartoum and then abroad. She lived alone in the house they had built together, tending her small garden, rising before dawn to walk the forest.

When the militia came through in the dry season of 2003, they came at night. Amara had been asleep when the first explosions shattered the darkness—not distant, but close enough that the walls of her house shook and plaster fell like ash onto her bed. She had crawled into the space beneath her kitchen table, her heart hammering so violently she thought it would break through her ribs. The sounds went on for hours: the crack and boom of ordnance, the sharp percussion of automatic weapons, voices shouting in languages she did not recognize. When men came through her door—she could not later say if they were looking for her specifically or simply moving through the village—she had remained motionless in the dark, her hand clamped over her mouth, certain that any sound, any movement, would mean her death. They had taken what they wanted and left. By morning, three of her neighbors' houses were burning.

She had left South Sudan four months later, on a visa sponsored by a church organization. She was fifty-four years old and had to begin again. An American forestry company hired her based on her credentials, and she had spent the last eighteen years working in the national forests of Oregon, living in a small town near the Wallowa-Whitman, doing the work she knew best in a landscape that was, at least, not her own.

But sleep had become impossible. For the first few years, Amara had simply accepted the insomnia—she would lie awake in the dark, her body rigid, listening to every creak of the old house. Then, about fifteen years into her time in America, she had begun turning on the television before bed. Just background noise, she told herself. Just to fill the silence. She would set it to a news channel or a cooking show, volume loud enough that she could not hear her own breathing, and eventually, somewhere around three in the morning, she would drift off to the murmur of voices and the blue glow of the screen. The habit had calcified. Now, at seventy-two, she could not sleep without it. If the power went out, or if she tried to lie in darkness, the old terror would surge back—her chest would tighten, her mind would race, and she would be back in that kitchen, waiting for footsteps.

Over time, the sensory distraction had become a kind of cage. She had come to depend on the noise—on having something external to anchor her attention—and without it, the darkness felt like an open door. Each night the television masked the silence, she reinforced the belief that silence itself was dangerous; the very strategy meant to soothe her had transformed ordinary quiet into a threat she now had to escape. But this very dependence had remade her world: the moments when the television failed to mask the silence became triggers in themselves, and the quiet hours that had once been ordinary—a power outage, a broken set—now carried the weight of threat. The strategy of filling silence with noise had created the very condition it was meant to prevent: silence itself had become something to fear. But this very dependence had remade her world: the moments when the television failed to mask the silence became triggers in themselves, and the quiet hours that had once been ordinary—a power outage, a broken set—now carried the weight of threat. Each night she managed to sleep through the noise, she reinforced the belief that silence itself was dangerous, until the absence of sound became as much a danger signal as the backfiring car or the slamming door. But the very act of relying on the television, of constantly needing to fill the silence, had made her more sensitive to the triggers themselves. When the power did occasionally fail, or when she found herself in an unexpectedly quiet moment, the contrast was so stark that the fear felt sharper, more immediate. And loud sounds—a car backfiring on the street outside, the bang of a door slamming in the wind—would send her into a state of acute alarm that could last for hours. She had learned to brace herself against these moments by staying vigilant, by constantly scanning her surroundings for signs of danger, watching people in the grocery store or at the ranger station for any hint of suspicious behavior. This hypervigilance, meant to keep her safe, had remade the world around her—every glance she cast, every person she assessed, every moment she spent braced for threat became a small confirmation that danger was everywhere, that her vigilance was justified, that she was right to be afraid. Her eyes were always moving, always assessing. At work, she found herself studying the contractors and visiting officials with an intensity that bordered on obsessive, noting who stood too close, who moved too quickly, whose intentions felt opaque.

Her colleagues had begun to notice. A younger forester named Marcus had mentioned, gently, that Amara seemed "on edge" during a recent field survey. She had snapped at him without meaning to—a sharpness born from the constant vigilance, from the exhaustion of never being able to truly relax. She had apologized, but something had shifted. Her hypervigilance in those moments—the way she monitored his movements, the tone of his voice—had created new triggers: the sight of Marcus approaching her desk now made her stomach tighten; the sound of footsteps in the hallway behind her sent her into alert; even the memory of that field survey became a place she could no longer bear to revisit, so she began inventing reasons to stay at the office during the hours when others were out in the field. She had started taking more solitary assignments, avoiding the team meetings where she felt exposed, unable to control the environment around her. But each time she chose the forest over the conference room, she was unknowingly narrowing her world—the very act of avoidance transformed ordinary workplaces into danger zones. The hallway she began to take the long way around, the meeting schedule she learned to dread before even opening her inbox, the sight of Marcus at his desk—these had all become triggers precisely because she had fled from them, because her safety lay in their absence. The hallway she began to take the long way around, the meeting schedule she learned to dread before even opening her inbox, the sight of Marcus at his desk—these had all become triggers precisely because she had fled from them, because her safety lay in their absence. Each time she declined a group assignment or found a reason to work alone in the forest, she reinforced a new landscape of avoidance—the conference room itself became a trigger, the sight of the meeting schedule in her inbox enough to set her heart racing, until even the possibility of being asked to attend a briefing sent her into a state of dread that lasted days. The places she avoided had become the places she feared most: by steering clear of the conference room, she had transformed it from a neutral workspace into a symbol of exposure and loss of control, and the longer she stayed away, the more catastrophic her imagination made it. Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of danger around her workplace—every corridor she took the long way around, every meeting she declined, every person she kept at a distance became a small confirmation that these things were indeed threats worth fearing.

It was her granddaughter, visiting from Portland, who had finally said something direct. She had found Amara in the kitchen at two in the morning, television blaring from the bedroom, and had asked, simply, "Grandmother, are you okay?" The question had broken something open. Amara had sat down at the table—the same table where she had hidden seventy years ago—and had begun, for the first time in decades, to speak about what had happened. Within a week, she had called the VA clinic. What frightened her most now was not the memory itself, but the way it had colonized her entire life, the way she had become a person who could no longer sit in silence, who could not trust the darkness, who was always, always waiting for the next explosion. She was hoping that someone could help her find her way back to sleep without the noise, back to the quiet, back to the person she had been before the fear had taken root.

She would set it to a news channel or a cooking show, volume loud enough that she could not hear her own breathing, and eventually, somewhere around three in the morning, she would drift off to the murmur of voices and the blue glow of the screen. The habit had calcified. Now, at seventy-two, she could not sleep without it. If the power went out, or if she tried to lie in darkness, the old terror would surge back—her chest would tighten, her mind would race, and she would be back in that kitchen, waiting for footsteps.

She had come to depend on the noise—on having something external to anchor her attention—and without it, the darkness felt like an open door. But this very dependence had remade her world: the moments when the television failed to mask the silence became triggers in themselves, and the quiet hours that had once been ordinary—a power outage, a broken set—now carried the weight of threat. Her eyes were always moving, always assessing. At work, she found herself studying the contractors and visiting officials with an intensity that bordered on obsessive, noting who stood too close, who moved too quickly, whose intentions felt opaque.

Her colleagues had begun to notice. A younger forester named Marcus had mentioned, gently, that Amara seemed "on edge" during a recent field survey. She had snapped at him without meaning to—a sharpness born from the constant vigilance, from the exhaustion of never being able to truly relax. She had apologized, but something had shifted. Her hypervigilance in those moments—the way she monitored his movements, the tone of his voice—had created new triggers: the sight of Marcus approaching her desk now made her stomach tighten; the sound of footsteps in the hallway behind her sent her into alert; even the memory of that field survey became a place she could no longer bear to revisit, so she began inventing reasons to stay at the office during the hours when others were out in the field. She had started taking more solitary assignments, avoiding the team meetings where she felt exposed, unable to control the environment around her. But each time she chose the forest over the conference room, she was unknowingly narrowing her world—the very act of avoidance transformed ordinary workplaces into danger zones. The hallway she began to take the long way around, the meeting schedule she learned to dread before even opening her inbox, the sight of Marcus at his desk—these had all become triggers precisely because she had fled from them, because her safety lay in their absence. Each time she declined a group assignment or found a reason to work alone in the forest, she reinforced a new landscape of avoidance—the conference room itself became a trigger, the sight of the meeting schedule in her inbox enough to set her heart racing, until even the possibility of being asked to attend a briefing sent her into a state of dread that lasted days. The places she avoided had become the places she feared most: by steering clear of the conference room, she had transformed it from a neutral workspace into a symbol of exposure and loss of control, and the longer she stayed away, the more catastrophic her imagination made it. Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of danger around her workplace—every corridor she took the long way around, every meeting she declined, every person she kept at a distance became a small confirmation that these things were indeed threats worth fearing.

It was her granddaughter, visiting from Portland, who had finally said something direct. She had found Amara in the kitchen at two in the morning, television blaring from the bedroom, and had asked, simply, "Grandmother, are you okay?" The question had broken something open. Amara had sat down at the table—the same table where she had hidden seventy years ago—and had begun, for the first time in decades, to speak about what had happened. Within a week, she had called the VA clinic. What frightened her most now was not the memory itself, but the way it had colonized her entire life, the way she had become a person who could no longer sit in silence, who could not trust the darkness, who was always, always waiting for the next explosion. She was hoping that someone could help her find her way back to sleep without the noise, back to the quiet, back to the person she had been before the fear had taken root.
